name: Dioxybenzone

lead: Dioxybenzone (benzophenone-8) is a UV filter that absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA, adding coverage that helps protect skin from sun aging. It appears in the US sunscreen monograph.

Its benzophenone core absorbs ultraviolet light and dissipates the energy, the same general mechanism as other benzophenone filters. Very little published research addresses it specifically, so its appearance benefit follows from sunscreens in general.

paras: It is used as one component in a combined filter system in sunscreens. Dedicated information on routines or results for dioxybenzone itself is sparse.

No dioxybenzone-specific human safety data appear in the sources. Studies of benzophenones as a class, mainly oxybenzone, have looked at environmental presence, coral toxicity and cell-level hormone activity.

web.title: Sunscreen: How to Help Protect Your Skin from the Sun - FDA

angle.text: Dioxybenzone (benzophenone-8) is a sunscreen filter in the US monograph that adds UVB and short-UVA coverage, protecting skin from sun-driven aging. It has almost no dedicated research, so its benefit is inferred from sunscreens as a class.

lead: Dioxybenzone, also called benzophenone-8, is a benzophenone-derived sunscreen ingredient that absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA light.[1] Sunscreen is the product category people use to keep skin from tanning, burning, pigmenting and ageing early, and dioxybenzone is one of the organic filters that has been listed for that job. Chemically it is (2-hydroxy-4-methoxyphenyl)(2-hydroxyphenyl)methanone, a yellow powder that is insoluble in water.[1] People use sunscreen to keep skin from tanning, burning, pigmenting and ageing early, which protects an even, youthful complexion; dioxybenzone is one of the organic filters that has been used in formulas for that purpose.

Wikipedia lists it among sunscreen agents approved by one or more agencies without naming which, and gives no safety or history information.[1] The US Food and Drug Administration's consumer page on sunscreen lists dioxybenzone among commonly used active ingredients and says that evidence shows at least some active ingredients are absorbed through the skin, so the agency has asked industry for data confirming their safety.[2]

Research on benzophenone UV filters as a class, mainly the better-known benzophenone-3 (oxybenzone), has examined environmental occurrence, hormone-related activity in cells and coral toxicity; dioxybenzone itself is rarely the subject of these studies, though a few include it among compounds tested.[3][4][5]
infobox: Insoluble in water; moderately soluble in ethanol and isopropanol[1]

paras: Dioxybenzone is an organic (chemical) filter: its benzophenone structure, with hydroxy and methoxy groups on a diphenyl ketone core, absorbs ultraviolet light [1]. It absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA [1]. Sunscreen formulas combine several filters to cover the UV spectrum; Wikipedia notes that SPF mainly reflects UVB protection, so UVA coverage depends on the filters chosen [6].

Dioxybenzone has a molar mass of about 244 g/mol, a density of about 1.38 g/cm3, a melting point of 68 C and a boiling point of 170 to 175 C. It is moderately soluble in ethanol and isopropanol and is a yellow powder at room temperature.[1]

It belongs to the benzophenone family, whose members share a diphenyl ketone core with hydroxy and methoxy substituents. These groups give the molecules their ability to absorb ultraviolet light, which is why the family appears in sunscreens and in plastics and coatings as UV stabilisers.

It is used as a sunscreen ingredient to absorb UVB and some UVA radiation.[1] The FDA's consumer sunscreen page names it among commonly used actives.[2] In the FDA's list of 17 active ingredients for products labelled as sunscreen, dioxybenzone appears alongside avobenzone, oxybenzone, octinoxate, octocrylene, homosalate, titanium dioxide, zinc oxide, ecamsule and others [2].

Sunscreen as a category matters to appearance because sun exposure is a leading cause of premature skin ageing. A 2013 Australian study of about 900 people reported smoother, more resilient skin after four and a half years of daily broad-spectrum sunscreen use, according to Wikipedia's sunscreen article.[6] Filters such as dioxybenzone are combined with others to give broad-spectrum coverage; UVA coverage in particular is a concern because conventional filters can block little UVA relative to their UVB-based SPF.[6]

FDA's consumer page says that for the most protection a broad-spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of at least 15 is recommended, and that SPF does not measure time in the sun: an SPF 15 product does not allow someone to stay out 15 times longer without burning [2].

In the United States, sunscreens are regulated as over-the-counter drugs. The FDA's page says that it has requested safety data from industry on active ingredients and lists dioxybenzone among them.[2] In the European Union, sunscreens are regulated as cosmetics, with minimum standards for SPF and UVA protection.[6]

The FDA page states that there is evidence that at least some sunscreen active ingredients are absorbed through the skin and enter the body, and that the agency needs to determine whether, and to what extent, this exposure carries safety risks; it does not describe specific absorption studies [2].

Benzophenone UV filters as a group have been measured in water, marine organisms and human samples.[3][7][8] A 2019 study tested four benzophenone filters, including BP-1, BP-3, BP-4 and BP-8 (dioxybenzone), on larvae and adults of two coral species, and a 2018 study examined thyroid-related activity of major benzophenones in cell lines and zebrafish embryos.[4][5] A 2024 survey measured baseline levels of oxybenzone, dioxybenzone and benzophenone in Biscayne National Park, Florida.[9] A 2020 study examined transfer of benzophenone-type UV filters from pregnant women to fetuses, and a 2011 method paper measured benzophenones in human placental tissue.[7][8]

Environmental surveys have measured organic UV filters in marine organisms, including seven filters in farmed fish and wild mussels from Hong Kong waters and filters in organisms from the South China Sea coastal region, where ecological risk was assessed [10][11]. The 2019 coral study tested BP-1, BP-3 (oxybenzone), BP-4 (sulisobenzone) and BP-8 (dioxybenzone) on larvae and adults of two coral species, reporting toxicity and bioaccumulation outcomes for the group [4]. A mini-review of benzophenone-3, the best-known member of the group, covers its occurrence, toxicities and ecological risks [3].
These studies concern the class and primarily its better-known members rather than dioxybenzone specifically.
No studies found. Studies of benzophenone filters in general are environmental or laboratory-based.[3][4][5]
